blocks.content: FOUNDATION OF THE INDIAN REPUBLIC

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Partition of India in 1947 caused unprecedented socio-economic dislocation and massive refugee rehabilitation challenges.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon successfully spearheaded the political unification of over 560 princely states into the Indian Union.
The Constituent Assembly framed the world's longest written constitution under the leadership of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
India established its foreign policy foundation on Non-Alignment, navigating the Cold War through strategic autonomy.
On January 26, 1950, the Constitution came into full force, formally transforming India into a Sovereign Democratic Republic.

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: India at the Midnight of Freedom

On 15 August 1947, India emerged as an independent nation after nearly 200 years of British colonial rule. However, independence did not mean stability or peace. The newly born nation faced one of the gravest crises in modern history. Partition had divided the country, millions were displaced, communal violence had shaken the social fabric, the economy was weak, administration was understaffed, and the future political structure of the nation was yet to be finalised. The period from 1947 to 1950 was therefore not merely a transitional phase but the foundation period that determined the political, administrative, economic, and constitutional character of modern India.
2. Partition of India (1947): Scale, Causes and Consequences

The partition of British India into two dominions—India and Pakistan—was accompanied by unprecedented violence and mass migration. Nearly 14–15 million people crossed borders, and around one million lost their lives. Communal hatred, rumours, fear, and administrative collapse turned partition into a humanitarian disaster.

• Communal polarisation during the colonial period

• Two-Nation Theory and political mobilisation

• Sudden announcement and hurried implementation of partition

• Absence of effective police and military control

• Breakdown of trust between communities

India faced the enormous task of rehabilitating millions of refugees arriving from Pakistan. The government set up relief camps, provided food and medical aid, and implemented policies to resettle refugees through land allotment, employment, and housing schemes. Evacuee property laws were enacted to redistribute abandoned properties.
3. Integration of Princely States: Political Unification of India

At independence, India was a fragmented political entity consisting of British provinces and 565 princely states. These states enjoyed varying degrees of autonomy under British suzerainty. Their integration into the Indian Union was essential to ensure political unity, national security, and administrative efficiency.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as the Home Minister, and V.P. Menon, as Secretary of the States Department, played a historic role in integrating princely states. They used diplomacy, persuasion, assurances, and, where necessary, force to achieve accession.
The Instrument of Accession was a legal document through which princely states agreed to join India, ceding control over defence, foreign affairs, and communications to the Union government.

Junagadh: Accession through plebiscite after Nawab’s decision was rejected.

Hyderabad: Operation Polo (1948) used military action to end Nizam’s rule.

Kashmir: Accession under extraordinary circumstances following tribal invasion.
4. Administrative and Political Reorganisation

Post-independence India had to reorganise its administrative structure to replace colonial institutions with national ones. The Indian Civil Service was transformed into the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), ensuring continuity as well as Indian control over governance.
5. Making of the Indian Constitution: Vision and Process

The framing of the Indian Constitution was one of the most ambitious exercises in democratic state-building. The Constituent Assembly represented the will of the Indian people and debated every aspect of governance to suit India’s social diversity and historical experience.

• First meeting: December 1946

• Dr. Rajendra Prasad – President of Constituent Assembly

• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar – Chairman of Drafting Committee

• Committees on Fundamental Rights, Union Powers, Minority Rights
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, a date chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj Declaration of 1930.

blocks.content: 6. Salient Features of the Indian Constitution (Explained)
The Indian Constitution established India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. It combined rigidity with flexibility and borrowed best features from global constitutions.

• Fundamental Rights ensuring equality and freedom

• Directive Principles guiding social and economic justice

• Parliamentary system based on British model

• Independent judiciary

• Federal structure with strong centre
7. Economic Challenges and Early Nation-Building

At independence, India inherited a stagnant economy characterised by poverty, illiteracy, low industrial growth, and agricultural backwardness. The leadership recognised the need for planned economic development.
The Planning Commission was set up to formulate Five-Year Plans and ensure balanced economic growth through state-led planning.
8. Foreign Policy Foundations: Non-Alignment
India adopted Non-Alignment to maintain independence in foreign policy during the Cold War. This policy was based on peaceful coexistence and opposition to military blocs.

items: Methods of integration: Junagadh (Plebiscite), Hyderabad (Operation Polo), and Jammu & Kashmir (Instrument of Accession).
Crucial Constituent Assembly dates: Objective Resolution (13 Dec 1946), Constitution Adopted (26 Nov 1949), Constitution Enforced (26 Jan 1950).
Important Constituent Assembly Committees: Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar), Union Powers Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru), Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Sardar Patel).

blocks.content: 9. India Becomes a Republic (1950)

On 26 January 1950, India became a Republic. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was sworn in as the first President, and the office of Governor-General was abolished, completing the transition from colony to sovereign republic.
10. Overall Significance of 1947–1950 Period

The period from 1947 to 1950 laid the institutional foundations of modern India. Political unity, constitutional democracy, secularism, and planned development became the pillars on which the Indian Republic was built.
